title: No Longer Slaves but Sons
summary: Paul compares life before Christ to an heir who, while still a child, is no better off than a slave. When the time had fully come, God sent his Son to redeem those under the law and sent the Spirit of his Son into believers' hearts, so they call God Abba, Father. Paul pleads with the Galatians not to return to slavery, recalls their warm welcome when he first came to them in illness, and closes with a figurative reading of Hagar and Sarah to show that believers are children of the free woman.
story: Chapter 3 ended with believers as Abraham's seed and heirs according to the promise. Chapter 4 explains what being an heir means and why going back under the law would be a step backward, from adult sonship into childhood and slavery. Paul's argument has a surprising edge: for these Gentile readers, taking on the law would be like returning to the pagan religion they left, since both put them under the weak and worthless principles of the world. In the middle of the chapter the argument gives way to a personal appeal, the most tender passage in the letter, before Paul returns to Scripture with the story of Abraham's two sons. The chapter prepares for the call to freedom that opens chapter 5.
historical:
Paul says he first preached to the Galatians because of an illness (v. 13), which apparently forced him to stay among them longer than he had planned. What the illness was is unknown. Some have guessed from verse 15, where he says they would have torn out their eyes for him, that it affected his eyesight, and some connect it with the thorn in the flesh of 2 Corinthians 12:7, but these are guesses; verse 15 may simply be an expression of devotion.

The phrase when the time had fully come (v. 4) reflects Paul's conviction that God chose the moment of Christ's coming. Christians later pointed to features of the first-century world that helped the gospel spread, such as the Roman peace, Roman roads, and the wide use of Greek, though Paul's own point is theological rather than historical: God's appointed time had arrived. The special days, months, seasons, and years of verse 10 most likely refer to the Jewish calendar of Sabbaths, new moons, and festivals that the Galatians were being urged to keep, though some scholars think Paul deliberately describes them in language that would also fit pagan calendars.
cultural:
Inheritance law shaped the picture in verses 1 and 2. In Roman and Greek households a minor who stood to inherit an estate was placed under guardians and managers until an age his father had set. Legally he owned everything; practically he had no more freedom than a household slave. Adoption as sons (v. 5) was a well-known Roman practice in which a man, often without an heir, legally took another person as his son with full rights of inheritance. Paul uses it to describe believers' new standing before God.

Abba is the Aramaic word for father, the language Jesus spoke. It was the word a child used at home, though adults used it too. Mark 14:36 records Jesus praying Abba, Father in Gethsemane, and Paul says that the Spirit of the Son now enables believers, even Greek-speaking Gentiles, to pray to God with the same word (v. 6; compare Romans 8:15). Welcoming a sick traveler, as the Galatians did, mattered in a culture where illness was sometimes read as a sign of divine displeasure; they could have treated Paul with contempt and did not (v. 14).
literary: The chapter mixes three kinds of writing. Verses 1 to 11 are argument by analogy (the heir under guardians), followed by a reversal: the Galatians, who know God or rather are known by God, are turning back. Verses 12 to 20 are personal appeal, full of emotion and imagery, including Paul's picture of himself as a mother in the pains of childbirth until Christ is formed in them. Verses 21 to 31 return to Scripture with a figurative reading of Genesis 16 to 21. Paul says these things serve as illustrations (v. 24), using a Greek verb from which the word allegory comes. He sets up two columns: Hagar the slave woman, Ishmael born according to the flesh, Mount Sinai, and the present Jerusalem on one side; Sarah the free woman, Isaac born through promise, and the Jerusalem above on the other. He quotes Isaiah 54:1, a promise to barren Jerusalem after exile, and Genesis 21:10, Sarah's demand to send Hagar away.

outline.t: From slaves to sons and heirs through the Son and the Spirit
Paul's personal appeal to his children
Hagar and Sarah: children of the slave woman and of the free

doctrines.note: Verses 4 to 6 show the Father sending the Son to redeem and sending the Spirit of his Son into believers' hearts. Salvation is the work of the one God, Father, Son, and Spirit, a pattern the church later confessed as the Trinity.
Salvation here is pictured as adoption: believers are brought from slavery into sonship, with the full rights of heirs. It rests on redemption, the Son's buying back of those under the law.
The Spirit is the Spirit of God's Son, and his presence is the proof of sonship. He cries out in believers' hearts, giving them the confidence of children who can call God Father.
God sent his Son, born of a woman, born under the law (v. 4). In one sentence Paul affirms that the Son existed to be sent, that he was truly human, and that he lived as a Jew under the law of Moses.

words.note: Huiothesia, adoption as sons. The word is used in the New Testament only by Paul, and it draws on the Roman legal practice of adoption, by which a person gained a new father, a new name, and full rights of inheritance. Believers are not naturally God's children in this sense but are made his children by grace, and are then as fully his heirs as a natural son.

Stoicheion, basic principle or element. The word could mean the letters of the alphabet, the elementary principles of a subject, or the physical elements (earth, water, air, fire), and some later writers used it for spirits associated with those elements or with the stars. Scholars debate which sense Paul intends in verses 3 and 9. What is clear is that he groups the Galatians' former pagan religion and a return to the law under the same heading: both are ways of living under something other than Christ.

Abba, the Aramaic word for father, carried over untranslated into Greek. It appears only three times in the New Testament (Mark 14:36, Romans 8:15, and here), always followed by the Greek word for father. It is often described as a child's word, and while it was not only a child's word, it did carry the intimacy of family speech. That believers pray with the same word Jesus used is a sign that they share his sonship.

Eleutheros, free. The word runs through the Hagar and Sarah passage (five times) and leads directly into chapter 5: believers are children of the free woman. Freedom in Galatians means release from slavery to the law, to sin, and to false gods, not permission to do anything at all.

christ: This chapter gives a compact account of who Christ is and what he has done. He is God's Son, sent by the Father at the appointed time, so he existed before he was born. He was born of a woman, fully human, and born under the law, sharing Israel's life and obligations. He came to redeem those under the law, buying them out of slavery, so that they might be adopted as God's children. Through him believers share his own relationship with the Father, praying Abba as he did. Paul's hope for the church is that Christ will be formed in them (v. 19), that his character will take shape in their life together.

hard.q: Is Paul's reading of Hagar and Sarah fair to Judaism, and to Hagar?
hard.a:
The passage is difficult on two counts. First, Paul links Mount Sinai and the present Jerusalem with slavery, which later Christians sometimes used to belittle Jews and Judaism. Many scholars point out that Paul's immediate targets were teachers inside the church who were pressing Gentile believers to be circumcised; on this reading the present Jerusalem stands for that movement and its base, not for Jewish people as such. Paul, himself a Jew, elsewhere insists that God has not rejected his people (Romans 11:1-2). Readers should resist turning the passage into a statement against Jews.

Second, Hagar in Genesis is a woman treated harshly by Abraham and Sarah, whom God sees, hears, and blesses (Genesis 16 and 21). Paul uses her only as a figure in an argument and does not retell her story. His reading is figurative and he says so. Interpreters differ on how far he means to make a claim about the original story, but most agree his point concerns two ways of relating to God, through slavery or through promise, not a verdict on Hagar herself.

questions: What difference does it make to think of yourself before God as a son or daughter and heir rather than as a hired servant?
Paul says the Galatians came to know God, “or rather are known by God.” Why might it matter that God's knowing you comes first?
Paul describes himself as a mother in labor until Christ is formed in his readers. Who has played that role in your life, and for whom might you?
